svg.aria-label: The lensless privacy ladder: what actually reduces identity leakage. Numbers from the 2026 lensless-gaze audit, arXiv 2609.09188, with a simulated fixed known PSF and 36-subject closed-set identification. Original eye crops give 97.7 percent top-1 identification. Raw simulated lensless measurements give 96.7 percent, so being unreadable to a human removes almost nothing. An MAE embedding retains 94.3 percent. An 8-dimensional PCA retains 93.2 percent and a matched 8-dimensional bottleneck 91.8 percent, so compression alone helps little. Separately trained 8-dimensional GSPL bottlenecks bring recovery down to 77.5 percent mean over three seeds. Beyond the audit's scope are defences that change the optics: low-resolution learned optical embeddings, shift-variant PSFs, and programmable masks that vary per capture as a key.
svg.title: Lensless privacy ladder — identity leakage by disclosure surface
svg.text: "Unreadable" is not "private": identity recovered from each disclosure surface
Top-1 identification, 36-subject closed set, simulated lensless gaze, fixed known PSF (arXiv 2609.09188, ECCV 2026 PFATCV workshop). Lower = more private.

g.text: Multiplexing is a known, invertible linear map — a learned adversary treats it as a change of basis. Compression alone barely helps; a trained bottleneck helps some.
Stronger defences change H itself (out of the audit's scope): low-res learned optical embeddings, shift-variant PSFs, or a programmable mask that varies per capture as a key.
